questions.title: Irreversible inhibition and substrate concentration
questions.question: In irreversible inhibition, increasing the concentration of substrate:

options.C: Has no effect on the reaction rate
options.D: Overcomes the inhibition, increasing the reaction rate up to 1/2 Vmax

explanations.A: Incorrect. Raising substrate concentration does not reverse an irreversible inhibitor's effect, so it cannot double the reaction rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adding more substrate does not itself further decrease the rate; the inhibition, once irreversibly established, simply is not overcome, but the rate does not fall further either.
explanations.C: Correct. An irreversible inhibitor permanently disables the fraction of enzyme molecules it binds, whether by chelating an essential cofactor, denaturing the protein, or blocking a chemical group required for catalysis. Because this loss of active enzyme is not competed away by substrate the way a competitive inhibitor's binding is, raising substrate concentration cannot restore the lost activity, and the reaction rate stays exactly where the irreversible inhibition left it. This lack of reversal by excess substrate is the defining functional difference between irreversible and competitive (reversible) inhibition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Overcoming inhibition by raising substrate concentration is the hallmark of competitive (reversible) inhibition, where more substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site; it does not happen with irreversible inhibition, where the enzyme is permanently disabled.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why raising substrate concentration cannot overcome irreversible enzyme inhibition, unlike competitive inhibition.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Has no effect on the reaction rate", p29

questions.title: False statement about enzymes
questions.question: Which of the statements regarding enzyme is false?

options.A: Enzymes are proteins that function as catalysts
options.D: Enzymes provide activation energy for reaction

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer (a true statement). Most enzymes are indeed proteins that function as biological catalysts, so this statement is true, not the false one being asked for.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer (a true statement). Enzyme activity is regulated in many ways, including allosteric effectors, covalent modification and changes in enzyme amount, so this statement is also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as an answer (a true statement). Enzymes are highly specific for their substrate or a narrow family of related substrates, so this statement is true as well.
explanations.D: Correct (the false statement). An enzyme does not provide or supply activation energy to a reaction; instead, it lowers the activation energy barrier that must be overcome, by stabilising the reaction's transition state, which is what allows the reaction to proceed faster at a given temperature. This distinction, between lowering a barrier and supplying energy, is exactly the point this false-statement item is testing. The reaction's own thermodynamics (its overall free energy change and equilibrium) are unaffected by the enzyme; only the rate at which equilibrium is reached changes.

questions.learning_objective: Correct the misconception that enzymes provide activation energy, instead of lowering the activation energy barrier.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Enzymes provide activation energy for reaction", p29

questions.title: Factor that does not affect enzymatic reaction rate
questions.question: On which of the following factors, does not affect the rate of enzymatic reaction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Substrate, enzyme and cofactor concentration all directly affect the rate of an enzymatic reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Temperature affects reaction rate, rising toward an optimum before the enzyme denatures at higher temperatures.
explanations.C: Correct. The molecular weight of the enzyme or substrate is not one of the recognised factors that governs the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. The rate is instead set by substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, cofactor concentration, temperature and pH, each of which changes the frequency or effectiveness of productive enzyme-substrate collisions or the enzyme's own catalytic conformation. Molecular weight, by contrast, is simply a physical property of the molecules involved and plays no direct role in that kinetic picture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. pH affects reaction rate, since most enzymes have an optimum pH range outside of which their ionisation state and structure are disturbed.

questions.learning_objective: Identify molecular weight as not one of the recognised factors affecting the rate of an enzymatic reaction.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Molecular weight", p30

questions.title: Enzyme concentration in a rate-versus-[S] plot
questions.question: When we discuss the relation between rate of reaction and [S], what should we do about the enzyme concentration?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Deliberately increasing enzyme concentration while plotting rate against [S] would confound the plot; it is held fixed, not increased.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Enzyme concentration is not simply irrelevant to the plot; it must be deliberately fixed so that [S] is the only variable changing.
explanations.C: Correct. When rate of reaction is plotted against substrate concentration [S] to study an enzyme's kinetics (as in deriving Km and Vmax), enzyme concentration must be held constant throughout, so that [S] is the only variable changing and the resulting curve reflects the enzyme's own kinetic behaviour rather than a confound from a shifting enzyme amount. If enzyme concentration were allowed to vary at the same time, the resulting rate-versus-[S] curve would not cleanly represent the enzyme's saturation kinetics. This controlled-variable principle is standard practice whenever a rate-versus-substrate curve is generated experimentally.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deliberately decreasing enzyme concentration during the plot would also confound the relationship being studied; it is held fixed, not decreased.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why enzyme concentration is held constant when plotting reaction rate against substrate concentration.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Remains constant", p30

questions.title: Factor giving a straight-line plot against reaction rate
questions.question: Which of the following factor when plotted against rate of reaction will form a straight line?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plot of rate against substrate concentration [S] is a curve that rises and then plateaus toward Vmax as the enzyme becomes saturated, not a straight line.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rate plotted against pH traces a bell-shaped curve around the enzyme's optimum pH, not a straight line.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Km is a fixed kinetic constant for a given enzyme-substrate pair, not a variable that is plotted against rate.
explanations.D: Correct. When substrate is present in excess (well above the concentration needed to saturate the enzyme), reaction velocity is directly proportional to enzyme concentration, so a plot of rate against enzyme concentration is a straight line through the origin. This direct proportionality is the basis for many clinical enzyme assays, where the measured rate is used to infer the amount of enzyme (and hence, for diagnostic enzymes, the extent of tissue damage) present in a sample. None of the other listed factors ([S], pH, Km) produce this simple linear relationship with rate.

questions.learning_objective: Identify enzyme concentration as the factor that gives a straight-line relationship with reaction rate under substrate-saturating conditions.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Enzyme reaction", p31

questions.title: Effect of temperature on reaction rate
questions.question: What is the effect of temperature on rate of reaction?

options.A: Increases till optimum temp and then decrease
options.C: No effect on rate of reaction

explanations.A: Correct. Raising temperature initially increases reaction rate, since molecules move faster and collide more frequently and energetically, up to the enzyme's optimum temperature (close to 37 degrees C for most human enzymes). Beyond that optimum, further heating denatures the enzyme's protein structure, disorganising the active site, and the rate falls sharply rather than continuing to rise. This rise-then-fall pattern, not a simple continuous increase or decrease, is the defining shape of an enzyme's temperature-rate curve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Temperature does not simply decrease reaction rate throughout its range; rate rises initially before falling only past the optimum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Temperature clearly affects reaction rate; it is not without effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rate does not simply keep increasing indefinitely with temperature; past the optimum, denaturation causes it to fall.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the rise-then-fall relationship between temperature and enzyme reaction rate around the optimum temperature.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Increases till optimum temp and then decrease", p31

questions.title: Effect of activators on reaction rate
questions.question: What is the effect of activators on rate of reaction?

explanations.A: Correct. An activator raises an enzyme's activity, either by increasing its affinity for substrate (lowering Km) or by raising its maximal catalytic activity (increasing Vmax), or both, which in turn increases the rate of the reaction it catalyses. A worked example is AMP acting as an allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 during glycolysis. This positive effect on rate is, by definition, the opposite of what an inhibitor does to the same enzyme.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decreasing rate is the effect of an inhibitor, not an activator; the two terms describe opposite effects on enzyme activity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An activator has one consistent direction of effect (increasing rate), not both directions at once.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An activator by definition does have an effect on rate; that is what makes it an activator.

questions.learning_objective: State that an activator increases the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Increase rate of reaction", p31

questions.title: Factor always inversely proportional to enzymatic reaction rate
questions.question: Which of the following factor is always inversely proportional to the rate of enzymatic reaction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Substrate concentration [S] is directly, not inversely, related to reaction rate (rate rises as [S] rises, up to saturation).
explanations.B: Correct. An inhibitor is, by definition, a substance that lowers enzyme activity, so raising inhibitor concentration always moves reaction rate in the opposite (inverse) direction, whether the mechanism is competitive, allosteric or irreversible. This inverse relationship holds consistently across inhibitor types, which is why inhibitors are the one factor among those listed that is always inversely, rather than directly or variably, related to rate. Substrate concentration, enzyme concentration and (within its optimum range) pH, by contrast, are all positively or non-monotonically related to rate rather than simply inverse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. pH's relationship to rate is bell-shaped around an optimum, not a simple inverse relationship.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enzyme concentration is directly, not inversely, proportional to reaction rate under substrate-saturating conditions.

questions.learning_objective: Identify inhibitors as the factor consistently inversely related to enzymatic reaction rate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Inhibitors", p32

questions.title: Raised LDH1 relative to LDH2
questions.question: An increase in serum level of LDH1 relative to LDH2 is an indication of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leukaemia is not the classic clinical setting associated with an LDH1-greater-than-LDH2 pattern (a "flipped" LDH ratio).
explanations.B: Correct. Lactate dehydrogenase is a tetramer of H (heart-type) and M (muscle-type) subunits, forming five isoenzymes, LDH1 (H4, cardiac-predominant) through LDH5 (M4, skeletal-muscle/liver-predominant). Normally LDH2 exceeds LDH1 in serum, so a rise in LDH1 to the point that it exceeds LDH2 (a "flipped" LDH1:LDH2 ratio) reflects cardiac muscle injury releasing its H-subunit-rich isoenzyme into the blood, classically myocardial infarction. This isoenzyme-ratio pattern is a tissue-specific diagnostic signal precisely because of LDH's differing subunit composition across tissues.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Muscular dystrophy would more classically raise LDH5 (M4, skeletal-muscle-predominant), not specifically flip the LDH1:LDH2 ratio.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hepatitis with jaundice is more classically associated with a rise in LDH5 (liver/skeletal-muscle-predominant) rather than a rise in the cardiac-predominant LDH1 isoenzyme.

questions.learning_objective: Interpret a flipped LDH1:LDH2 serum ratio as indicating myocardial injury such as infarction.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Myocardial infarction", p32

questions.title: Multiple forms of the same enzyme
questions.question: Multiple forms of the same enzyme is referred to as:

explanations.A: Correct. Isoenzymes (isozymes) are multiple physically distinct forms of the same enzyme, each catalysing the same reaction but differing in their amino acid sequence, kinetic properties, or tissue distribution. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH1-LDH5, built from H and M subunits) and creatine kinase (CK-MM, CK-MB, CK-BB, built from M and B subunits) are the classic worked examples, and their differing tissue distribution is exactly what makes measuring a specific isoenzyme fraction diagnostically useful. This term specifically names the phenomenon of one catalytic function being carried out by more than one molecular form of enzyme.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A biosensor is a device that uses a biological component (often an enzyme) to detect a chemical substance; it is not the term for multiple forms of one enzyme.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An allosteric enzyme is one regulated by an effector binding away from its active site; it describes a regulatory property, not the existence of multiple forms of the same enzyme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Effectors are molecules (activators or inhibitors) that bind an allosteric site and modulate enzyme activity; they are not the term for multiple forms of the same enzyme.

questions.learning_objective: Define isoenzymes as multiple distinct molecular forms of the same enzyme.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Isoenzyme", p32
